input:
This executive summary presents an overview of the delivery performance of a contract packaging firm that operates 3 plants and generates revenue of $103 million per year. The analysis is based on a comprehensive review of the order records for a period of 12 months, encompassing a total of 12292 orders, and it paints a picture of a business whose delivery performance has been deteriorating in a number of important respects.

Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery has averaged 88%, which falls noticeably short of the target of 95% that the business has set for itself. The problem is heavily concentrated in one part of the business: Plant 2 is responsible for no less than 62% of all late orders. At the same time, the order backlog has grown to 3.4 weeks, compared with 1.8 weeks a year ago, and overtime costs have risen to $1.4 million last year, representing an increase of 27% on the year before.

In order to address this situation, the installation of a scheduling system is under consideration. A system covering all plants has been quoted at $332k, while the cost of installing the system at Plant 2 alone would be $127k. According to an internal estimate, which it should be emphasised is not a vendor figure, the installation at Plant 2 could be expected to reduce overtime at that plant by some 15-20% during the first year of operation.

Against this background, the recommendation that is currently under consideration is that the system should be installed at Plant 2 in the first instance, with the other plants held back until the results from Plant 2 have been reported and evaluated. The scheduling programme as a whole is owned by the operations director, who will be responsible for reporting the outcomes of the initial installation.
target:
Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, and hold the other plants until the Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The firm runs 3 plants on revenue of $103 million per year, and delivery performance has fallen behind the level the order book requires: the question this summary answers is where the failure sits and what to fund first.

The evidence base is the order records for 12 months, covering 12292 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 88%, against a target of 95%. Plant 2 accounts for 62% of late orders, and the failure is concentrated there rather than spread across the firm. The backlog stands at 3.4 weeks, against 1.8 weeks a year ago, and overtime cost was $1.4 million last year, up 27% on the year before. The pattern holds across both quarters in the evidence base, and the concentration of late orders in one plant is a property of the records, not of the sampling.

A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $332k, and Plant 2 alone is $127k. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The staged install takes the reduction where the late orders sit, at the single-plant price, and defers the remaining spend until the result is in.

The hold on the other plants is part of the recommendation, not a deferral of it: the spend on the remaining plants is committed only when the first install has reported, and the overtime and backlog figures above are the measures on which that report will be judged. The programme is judged on reported results, and the report is the decision point for the remaining plants.
